nameStory: The 'sundragon' name comes from this dragonfly's habit of basking in sunny spots, where its metallic body gleams like burnished metal in the light. It's named after Philip Reese Uhler, a 19th-century American entomologist who was one of the first scientists to systematically study dragonflies and other insects in North America.
description: Uhler's Sundragon is a medium-sized dragonfly with a dark, metallic body that shimmers with bronze and green highlights in sunlight. Adults typically measure about 2 to 2.5 inches long with a wingspan around 3 inches. Like other emerald dragonflies, they have relatively broad bodies and are strong, agile fliers. Their eyes are large and prominent, giving them excellent vision for hunting small flying insects.

idTips.label: Metallic body sheen
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen have a distinctive dark metallic luster that shifts between bronze, green, and copper tones depending on the angle of sunlight - like looking at an oil slick

idTips.label: Broad, sturdy build
idTips.description: Noticeably stockier and more robust-looking than many other dragonflies, with a thick thorax that feels solid if you gently handle one

idTips.label: Clear wings with dark veins
idTips.description: Wings are transparent with prominent dark veining, and may have a slight amber or yellowish tint, especially near the base

idTips.label: Large compound eyes
idTips.description: Eyes are proportionally large and touch at the top of the head, appearing almost metallic green or bronze up close

idTips.label: Sun-seeking behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on sun-warmed rocks, logs, or bare ground in open sunny areas, returning repeatedly to the same favorite spots

habitat: Look for Uhler's Sundragon around ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and marshy areas throughout New England, especially where there are adjacent sunny clearings or meadows. They prefer areas with some emergent vegetation like cattails or sedges for egg-laying, but spend much of their time hunting in open spaces nearby.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually May, but are not yet at peak activity. Look for fresh individuals with pristine wings near water where they developed as nymphs.
seasonality.summer: Peak flying season from June through August. Most active on warm, sunny days when they're easiest to spot perching in open areas and patrolling territories over water.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with some individuals flying into September. Late-season adults may appear slightly worn with small tears or fading in wing membranes.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - they overwinter as nymphs (juveniles) underwater in ponds and streams, where they continue growing beneath the ice.

funFact: Uhler's Sundragon nymphs are aquatic predators that can actually shoot water out of their rear end like a jet engine to escape danger - they suck water into their gill chamber and then forcefully expel it for rapid underwater propulsion!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark, metallic dragonflies in the emerald family, but Uhler's Sundragon has a distinctly broader, more robust build than most relatives. Remember: 'Uhler's is ULTRA-broad' - the stocky body shape is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: Philip Uhler, this species' namesake, was a pioneering American entomologist who worked at Johns Hopkins University and described many North American insects for the first time. The scientific study of dragonflies was still quite new when this species was named in his honor in the late 1800s.
compareHints: As the only sundragon species in our region, compare Uhler's Sundragon to other emerald dragonflies like the American Emerald or racket-tailed emeralds. Uhler's has a notably broader, more robust body build and tends to perch more often in sunny spots away from water, while other emeralds are typically more slender and stay closer to their aquatic habitats.
